Deployment Hosting: Bare Metal, IaaS and PaaS (Section 10.2)

Tutorial: Deploying on a PaaS provider (Heroku)
Section point: something the chapter states directly. Expect these in quizzes and exams.

sections.title: Where Week 10 fits in the software life cycle

blocks.text: In earlier weeks you followed the software development life cycle (SDLC) from requirements to design to development (frameworks, IDEs, debugging and code-analysis tools) to testing (unit testing up to whole-system testing). Week 10 covers what happens after the software has been built and tested:
Deployment means “placing” the software system so that its users can easily access it. A web application, for example, has to be hosted on a server somewhere so that users can reach it through a URL.
Monitoring means capturing and analysing information about the application while it runs: how users are using it, and whether there are performance problems, errors, timeouts and so on.
Section point: Deployment = making the built system accessible to its users. Monitoring = capturing and analysing an application’s execution information after it has been deployed.

blocks.caption: The big picture of Week 10: develop and test the software, deploy it so real users can reach it, then monitor how it behaves and feed what you learn back into development.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Where Week 10 fits in the software life cycle

blocks.text: What is an environment?
Section point: An environment is a system, or a set of systems, that executes a software application.
Developers write and test code, and an environment builds that code into something that runs and that users or other people can access. A software team usually works with four kinds of environment:
Development environment
Testing environment
Staging environment
Production environment
Not every team has all four, but development, testing and production are almost always present. Staging is very common and strongly recommended. The code moves through the environments in this order:
Development → Testing → Staging → Production

blocks.caption: The four environments in order: 1. Development (write code), 2. Testing (find bugs), 3. Staging (rehearse the release on a copy of production), 4. Production (real users).

blocks.text: 1.1 Development environment
The development environment is the local environment of an individual software developer: their own machine, with an IDE and whatever other tools they like to use.
In this environment the developer:
writes code,
tests it (unit tests),
builds the code base to check that it compiles and works, and
commits the code to the shared code base kept in a version control system (such as Git).
Two terms from the example diagrams are important:
Working copy: the developer’s own copy of the code base on their machine.
Mainline / master branch: the shared code base in version control that everybody commits to.
Before or while committing, the developer must check that their working copy does not clash (conflict) with changes other developers have already made to the mainline. Any conflicts must be resolved.
The development environment is also connected to a local database. The developer can freely read from and write to it without affecting the real data of the live system.

blocks.caption: Development environment: a developer writes, runs, tests and builds code locally (with an IDE and a local database), then commits and pushes it to the shared repository’s main branch, which other developers also use.

blocks.text: 1.2 Testing environment

When developers have written and unit-tested their code, the code in the shared repository is placed in the testing environment. Here, integration testing and system testing are carried out: the pieces written by different people are tested together, and then the system is tested as a whole.

blocks.caption: Testing environment: code from the shared repository is deployed as a test build with its own test database, software tests are run, and bugs found (here in the cart) are reported back as defects.

blocks.text: If a test fails, the chapter describes this procedure:
The defective code is removed from the testing environment.
The module in which the failure occurred is identified.
The developer responsible for that module is identified and notified.
The code in the testing environment is rolled back to the previous working version.
The responsible developer fixes the bug in their own working copy and commits it to the shared code base again.
The fixed code reaches the testing environment in the next scheduled deployment.
1.3 Staging environment
Once the code has been tested thoroughly, can it go straight to users? Usually it first goes to a staging environment.
Section point: Staging is a pre-production environment; it exactly resembles the production environment in hardware, software and configuration, and runs on a remote machine.
Reflection: why not push directly to production?
Think about this before reading on. The chapter gives three reasons for having a staging environment.

Deployment is complicated and risky. Deploying involves many activities and configurations: installing libraries and packages, configuring them, running scripts (for example, initialising the database). The same is true when updating modules or adding features to a live application. If this is done directly in production and something goes wrong, the live system can crash and affect real users. Doing it first in staging, an exact replica, shows whether the installation and updates work. Successful rehearsal reduces release risk; it does not guarantee a safe production release.
Previewing new features. Staging is a good place to show new features to management, the sales or marketing team, or a client, without releasing them to everyone.
Performance and stress testing cannot be done locally or in the testing environment. Doing it in production would affect users, so staging is used.

blocks.caption: Without staging, a new version released directly to production can break the live site for real users. With staging, a bug (here in the cart) is found and fixed before release, and users get a working store.

blocks.text: 1.4 Production environment
The production environment, also called the live environment, is where the software actually runs for all its users. Users interact with it directly, and it holds real data.

blocks.caption: After tests pass and staging is verified, the application is deployed to the production environment, which serves real users. Monitoring the live system feeds performance information back to the team.

blocks.text: What happens when a new feature is requested?

Suppose the application is live and working, and the client asks for a new feature (a new user interface, say). The team goes through one more iteration of the life cycle: design, then development. Each developer modifies the code in their working copy, tests it and commits it to the shared code base, and the change passes through testing → staging → production again.

The last step, moving the new version from staging into production, needs care, because production is the system people are using right now. The move must be smooth. The planned way of doing it is called a deployment strategy.
Section point: Deployment strategies are ways of pushing code from the staging environment to the production environment. The chapter covers three: Blue/Green, Canary and Versioned deployment.
2.1 Blue/Green deployment (Staged deployment)
Idea: create a new, separate production environment for the new version, without affecting the current one.
How it works:
The Blue environment is the current live production environment. A router sends all users to it.
The new version is deployed to a second, identical production environment called Green. No users are sent there yet.
Green is tested thoroughly (integration testing and other testing).
The router switches all incoming requests from Blue to Green. Green is now live, and Blue sits idle.

blocks.caption: Before the switch: the router sends 100% of live traffic to BLUE (Version 1). GREEN (Version 2) has been deployed, tested and verified but receives no live traffic yet.
After the switch: the router now sends 100% of live traffic to GREEN (Version 2), which is monitored, while BLUE (Version 1) is kept on standby as a rollback option.

blocks.text: Main advantage — easy rollback. If something goes wrong after the switch (errors, or the system crashes), the router simply sends users back to Blue, which is known to work.

blocks.caption: Rollback: an issue is found in GREEN (Version 2), so the router sends 100% of traffic back to BLUE (Version 1) while the team investigates Green.

blocks.text: Regular cycling. The two environments take turns. If Green is live now, the next update is pushed from staging to Blue, and then the router switches to Blue. Blue and Green keep alternating between “real (live)” and “previous version”.
2.2 Canary deployment (Phased rollout / Incremental rollout)
Idea: instead of sending all users to the new version at once, slowly roll out the change to a small subset of users first, and increase the share step by step.
The name comes from the “canary in a coal mine”: a small early warning before everyone is exposed.

blocks.caption: Canary deployment: the traffic router sends 95% of users to the stable Version 1 and 5% to the canary Version 2, which the team monitors closely.

blocks.text: How are the users for the new version chosen? The chapter lists these options:
Randomly
By user profile or demographics
By region: if there are servers in different locations, roll out to one region first, check that it works properly there, then roll out to other regions incrementally.

blocks.caption: Canary traffic increases gradually: 5% canary traffic first, then 25%, then 100%, with performance checked before each step.

blocks.text: Drawback: you must manage multiple instances at once. Some users are on the old version and some on the new one, so both have to be run and supported at the same time.

blocks.caption: Blue/Green switches all traffic between two environments at once; Canary starts with a small portion of traffic (e.g. 5%) and gradually increases it while monitoring response time and error rate.

blocks.text: 2.3 Versioned deployment
Idea: allow users to choose which version to use, and keep all versions alive.
This is common in mobile apps (the chapter’s examples are Paytm and Instagram). You get a notification that an update is available:
if you update, you are routed to the new version;
if you don’t, you continue on the previous version.

Drawback: the company has to maintain multiple versions, because not all users update regularly. Companies therefore announce that only certain versions are supported up to a given date, after which older versions stop receiving support.

blocks.caption: Versioned deployment: users choose; all versions kept alive
blocks.alt: Versioned deployment: users choose; all versions kept alive

blocks.text: What is hosting?
Hosting is the infrastructure required to host (deploy) an application. Web applications are usually hosted on server systems, and clients access the application from the server.

Section point: An important characteristic of hosting, especially for production, is that the system must be available all the time — 24 hours a day, throughout the year, with no unplanned downtime — and user data must be stored securely, because real users and real data are involved.
The chapter compares three hosting options:
Bare metal servers
Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS)
Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS)

blocks.caption: Three hosting options: who sets up which layer
blocks.alt: Three hosting options: who sets up which layer

blocks.text: A helpful way to remember them is the stack drawn on the slides. Every hosted web application needs four layers:
Server Hardware → Operating System → Web Server → Web Application
The three options differ in how many of these layers you set up yourself.
3.1 Bare metal servers
With bare metal you buy the actual server hardware and set up everything yourself: the operating system, the web server and the web application, which means all four layers.
A server has the same basic parts as a desktop (CPU, motherboard, RAM, disk), but in much higher configurations and with server-specific features.
Servers come in compact forms such as rack servers and blade servers, so that many can be stacked in a rack.
Advantage: Highest performance (exclusive access, not shared).
Disadvantages:
Most expensive upfront. Servers can cost lakhs of rupees.
Time and effort to set up hardware, OS, web server and application.
Ongoing maintenance (time, effort and money), for example when a part fails and must be repaired.

blocks.caption: Bare metal: the company owns the physical server, manages hardware maintenance, the operating system, software installation and network security itself, and serves the web application over the internet.

blocks.text: 3.2 Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS)
An IaaS provider buys the server hardware, configures it, and rents you a part of that infrastructure for a fee.

Section example: An IaaS provider has a server with an 8-core processor and 32 GB RAM. It slices this into 8 parts, and each part is a virtual machine (VM) with 1 core and 4 GB of memory. You get exclusive access to your VM, and on it you set up your web server, database and application.
In terms of the stack, the provider gives you the hardware (as a VM) with an operating system. You set up the web server and web application.
Examples: DigitalOcean, AWS, Linode.

blocks.caption: IaaS slices an 8-core, 32 GB server into 8 VMs of 1 core and 4 GB
blocks.alt: IaaS slices an 8-core, 32 GB server into 8 VMs of 1 core and 4 GB

blocks.text: Advantages:
Cheaper.
No maintenance overhead.
Disadvantages:
Each IaaS provider has its own set of configurations (CPU, memory options, etc.). You must learn them and check that they suit your application.
The infrastructure is shared by others, so performance may suffer compared with your own dedicated server.
3.3 Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS)
A PaaS provider automatically sets up the web server and database; you provide configuration options.
In terms of the stack, the provider handles hardware, OS and web server. You only provide the web application.
Examples: Heroku, Google App Engine.
Advantage: very easy to deploy. Give it your code and it takes care of setting up the web server, database server and so on.
Disadvantage: lack of control. You don’t know or control the underlying OS, hardware or configuration.
3.4 Comparing the three options

rows: A virtual machine (slice of a server)
Automatically sets up the web server and database; you provide configuration options
Web server, database, app (on the VM)
Most expensive upfront, setup and maintenance effort
Provider-specific configurations; shared, so performance may suffer

blocks.caption: Bare metal, IaaS and PaaS: advantages and disadvantages
blocks.alt: Bare metal, IaaS and PaaS: advantages and disadvantages

blocks.text: The next two parts are the tutorials, which show IaaS and PaaS in practice. The picture below previews the difference between them.

blocks.caption: IaaS vs PaaS workflow: on DigitalOcean you create the VM, configure the OS, install dependencies and deploy the app yourself; on Heroku you prepare the app and push the code, and the platform builds and runs it.

blocks.text: DigitalOcean is an IaaS provider. It gives you the hardware and the operating system on which to host your application.
Key term: Droplet
Section point: A Droplet is DigitalOcean’s term for a virtual machine.
The droplet shown in the chapter (it hosts the verisim web page) had 1 GB memory, 25 GB disk, and ran Ubuntu 18.04. From the dashboard you can monitor bandwidth, CPU usage, disk I/O and so on.
Creating a droplet, step by step

blocks.caption: Creating a DigitalOcean Droplet: (1) click Create Droplet, (2) choose a region / data centre such as Bangalore, (3) choose the configuration — OS, CPU and RAM, (4) configure access (SSH authentication), (5) launch — the cloud VM is running.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Part 4 — Tutorial: IaaS with DigitalOcean

blocks.text: Log in / sign up and create (or open) a project, giving it a name, description and purpose. Existing resources can be moved into it if needed.
Create a droplet.
Choose a region (data centre). The example chooses Bangalore, closest to us.
Choose the operating system and version (e.g. Ubuntu).
Choose the droplet type / plan.
A basic droplet is enough for simple applications such as blogs, discussion forums and small projects.
CPU options: regular, or premium Intel/AMD.
Shared CPU vs dedicated CPU.

Plans range up to very large machines (around 256 GB RAM and multi-terabyte storage in the chapter). The price is calculated per month, starting from about $6/month at the time of the chapter. Extra storage can be added.
The illustration below shows the droplet configuration options.

blocks.caption: Shared CPU vs dedicated CPU: with a shared CPU, several VMs take turns on the same processor cores; with a dedicated CPU, cores are reserved for your VM only — more predictable performance at a higher price.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Part 4 — Tutorial: IaaS with DigitalOcean

blocks.text: Choose the authentication method:
SSH key: connect securely from your own terminal; or
Password.
Optional extras: enable monitoring and backups.
Create the droplet, then log in with the credentials you set.
Connecting to the droplet with SSH

blocks.caption: Connect to the DigitalOcean Droplet from a terminal using SSH, then log in and deploy the application as on a local system.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Part 4 — Tutorial: IaaS with DigitalOcean

blocks.text: Deploying the application on the droplet

Section point: After logging in to the droplet you deploy just as you would on your local system: check out the code (e.g. from GitHub), set up the web server and database server, and run the application. With IaaS, all of this is your job.

blocks.caption: The full IaaS lifecycle on DigitalOcean: create a droplet (choose region, CPU, RAM, storage), configure the server over SSH (OS, application setup, network and security), then monitor CPU, memory, disk and network usage.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Part 4 — Tutorial: IaaS with DigitalOcean

blocks.text: The droplet dashboard also shows live resource graphs. This is your first taste of monitoring, covered fully in Part 7.

blocks.caption: After deployment, monitor the VM: CPU, memory, disk and network graphs reveal problems such as high CPU usage, which you then inspect, investigate and act on.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Part 4 — Tutorial: IaaS with DigitalOcean

blocks.text: Heroku is a PaaS provider: it provides the entire platform (the infrastructure and an easy way to deploy). The tutorial deploys a very simple Flask application with one route that displays “Hello World”.

blocks.caption: Running locally vs deployed on Heroku: locally, Flask’s development server runs the app at http://127.0.0.1:5000 for the developer only; after deployment, Heroku runs it on a cloud platform accessible over the internet.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Part 5 — Tutorial: PaaS with Heroku

blocks.text: Overview of the steps

blocks.caption: Deploying to Heroku: (1) create the Flask app, (2) prepare the files — requirements.txt and Procfile, (3) create the Heroku app, (4) push the code with git, which builds and deploys it, (5) the live web app is accessible to users.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Part 5 — Tutorial: PaaS with Heroku

blocks.text: Step 1 — Prepare the application

(a) Create a virtual environment. This keeps the project’s packages separate, so they do not conflict with other packages on your system. Activate it. Running pip freeze at this point shows nothing installed.

python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate   # Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
pip freeze                 # shows nothing yet
(b) Install the needed modules: Flask and Gunicorn.
pip install flask gunicorn
Section point: Gunicorn is a Web Server Gateway Interface (WSGI) server. Heroku uses it to run Python web applications.
Installing these also pulls in some other packages they depend on. pip freeze now lists all the packages with their versions.
(c) Save the dependency list in requirements.txt.
pip freeze > requirements.txt
requirements.txt is the list of packages (with version numbers) the project needs. Heroku reads it and installs exactly those packages and versions.
(d) Create the Procfile. The Procfile tells Heroku how to run the application. For this app it contains one line:
web: gunicorn app:app
Read it as: “this is a web application; run it with the gunicorn server; in the file app.py there is a variable called app (the Flask object), and that is what must be run.”
Section point: requirements.txt (what to install) and the Procfile (how to run) are the two important settings you must prepare for Heroku.

blocks.caption: The two Heroku settings: requirements.txt lists the Python dependencies (Flask, gunicorn) — what to install; the Procfile (web: gunicorn app:app) is the startup command — how to run the app. Heroku installs the packages and starts the web process.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Part 5 — Tutorial: PaaS with Heroku

blocks.text: Step 2 — Create an app on Heroku
Sign up or log in on the Heroku website.
Click New → Create new app, give it a name and choose a region (the example chose Europe).
Heroku’s documentation on running Python apps (installing dependencies, the Procfile) is available online and was used to set up the app.
Step 3 — Deploy using the Heroku CLI and Git
Heroku offers several ways to deploy. The tutorial uses the Heroku command-line interface (CLI):

heroku login                      # opens a browser to log in
git init                          # start a git repository
heroku git:remote -a <app-name>   # add remote "heroku"
git add Procfile app.py requirements.txt
git commit -m "initial commit"
git push heroku master

runs.text: heroku login                      # opens a browser to log in
git init                          # start a git repository

blocks.text: The key idea is that Heroku is the git remote. Instead of pushing to GitHub, you push your master branch to Heroku. Only the project files are added; the virtual-environment folder is not.

blocks.caption: Deploying to Heroku using Git: prepare the Flask app, create an app through New → Create new app (Europe), connect Git with heroku git:remote -a <app-name>, commit, then run git push heroku master. Heroku builds and deploys the application.
blocks.alt: Five steps for deploying a Flask Hello World application to Heroku using the master branch.

blocks.text: Pushing does two things: it uploads the code, and it starts the deployment. In the build output you can watch Heroku:
install Python and pip,
install everything listed in requirements.txt,
read the Procfile, understand that this is a web application, and launch it.
Open the given URL in a browser and the app (“Hello World”) is live.
Step 4 — The Heroku dashboard
On the Heroku website you can see that the build succeeded and the app is deployed. Heroku also provides:
Metrics: in the chapter these required adding a credit card.
Resources / add-ons: data stores, caching, content management and more.

blocks.caption: The Heroku dashboard: application overview (status Running), controls (Overview, Resources, Settings, Activity), and status checks — web process, recent release and logs.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Part 5 — Tutorial: PaaS with Heroku

blocks.text: Step 5 — Deploying an update
Updating is just the normal git commit process. For example, change the message to “Hello World new version”, then:

git status
git add app.py
git commit -m "change the message"
git push heroku master
Heroku rebuilds and redeploys automatically. Refresh the browser to see the new version.

blocks.caption: Updating a Heroku app: (1) change the code, (2) commit and push to the Heroku Git remote, (3) Heroku builds, releases and runs the new version, (4) check the live application to verify the update.
blocks.alt: Illustration: Part 5 — Tutorial: PaaS with Heroku

blocks.text: Section point: Other PaaS platforms, such as Google App Engine, follow a similar process.
Why CI?

blocks.caption: What is Continuous Integration? Developers frequently push code to a shared Git repository; the CI pipeline automatically builds and tests every change; developers get quick feedback (checks passed or failed) and fix problems early.

blocks.text: Deployment is important but time-consuming. Code written by many people must be integrated, tested sufficiently and deployed correctly to the live environment without bugs. Doing all of this by hand for every change is slow and error-prone.

blocks.caption: Without CI, developers integrate late: merge conflicts pile up, the application breaks and bugs are discovered late. With CI, each developer’s change goes through the pipeline (commit, build, test) frequently, so problems are found early.

blocks.text: Continuous integration is a way of automating the integration and deployment of software applications.
The CI process (7 steps)
Three systems are involved:
Version Control System (VCS): stores the versions of the code.
Continuous Integration server: automatically builds and tests the code.
Staging / Deployment server: where the code is finally deployed.
The steps, exactly as on the slide:
Developer commits code to the version control system (after writing and testing it locally).
The CI server pulls the new code after each commit.
The CI server builds and tests the code automatically, running unit and integration tests and checking for errors.
If there are no errors, the CI server tells the staging/deployment server that the code is ready to deploy.
The deployment server pulls the code from the version control system.
The deployment server does one more round of building and testing, and deploys it.
The deployment server notifies the CI server that deployment is complete.
Building, testing, integrating and deploying are all automated with scripts and the CI server.

blocks.caption: The continuous integration process

blocks.text: Best practices for CI (7 practices)
Memorise these seven; the chapter summary lists exactly these.
1. Maintain a single source repository. Keep one mainline (master) branch, and most people should work on it most of the time. A few branches for trying new features or fixing bugs are fine.

2. Automate the build. A build involves compiling, copying and moving files, creating database schemas and so on. Build tools automate this once you write scripts with the correct configuration. The chapter’s examples: Ant and Gradle for Java, and “Builder” for Node.js.

blocks.caption: Automating the build: when code is pushed, the CI build job installs dependencies, runs the build steps and checks the result — producing a build artifact if the build passes.

blocks.text: 3. Make the build self-testing. Create automated tests that check a large part of the code base. A simple command should run the whole test suite, and when a test fails, a notification should be sent to the developer responsible for that module.

blocks.caption: A self-testing build: the CI test job runs unit tests (individual units of code) and integration tests (interactions between components) on the built application; if tests fail, the developer investigates, fixes the code and pushes again.

blocks.text: 4. Commit to the main branch every day. Before committing, developers write code, write tests, build, check for errors and check for conflict errors, which happen when someone else has already modified the same parts of the code. - Infrequent commits → more chances of conflict errors. - Frequent commits encourage developers to break their work into very small chunks.

5. Every commit should build the main branch on an integration server. The CI server monitors the repository. On every commit it pulls the new code, builds it, runs integration tests, and tells the committer whether everything works. If all tests pass, the build is successful. - Examples of CI servers: Jenkins and CruiseControl. (The chapter shows a CruiseControl dashboard listing recent builds, which passed or failed, how long they took and who made the changes.)
6. Fix broken builds immediately (a priority for developers): take the system back to the last-known good build so others are not affected, then fix the bug.
7. Automate deployment. Write scripts that deploy automatically, for example to the staging environment. This ensures that the latest code is always available in staging.

blocks.caption: Pipeline passed vs pipeline failed: when all checks pass, a build artifact is produced and is ready for the next step; when a test fails, the developer investigates, fixes and retries — a broken build is fixed immediately.

blocks.text: Reflection: what are the benefits of CI?
Think about benefits for end users, developers and the organisation before reading the chapter’s answer.
Reduces deployment time. Building, testing and deploying are automated with scripts and the integration server, which minimises the steps needing human intervention.

Avoids last-minute confusion and rush at release dates. Without CI, developers may not commit for weeks or months and then all commit just before a deadline, causing many conflicts. CI requires daily commits, so conflicts stay small.
Beneficial to users. An updated copy of the software is always available on the staging server, so users can see an initial prototype, and the sales or management team can give a demo at any time.
Beneficial to developers. Committing small pieces frequently pushes developers to write more efficient, modular code.
Drawback: the initial effort needed to set up the processes, set up the integration server and train people. In most cases the advantages far outweigh this.

blocks.caption: Benefits and drawback of continuous integration
blocks.alt: Benefits and drawback of continuous integration

blocks.text: Once the code is deployed, we must make sure the application performs to an acceptable standard. The chapter covers three ways to improve performance:
Caching
Task queues
Making pages load and render quickly

blocks.caption: Slow website vs fast website: a slow store makes users wait, frustrates them and may make them leave; a fast store gives a quick response, happy users and smooth shopping.

blocks.text: 7.1 Caching

Section point: Caching stores the results of common operations in memory, which reduces the load on servers. Instead of fetching data from the database every time, it is fetched from memory, which is faster.
If the same queries run again and again, and the database has not changed, their results can be stored in memory and served from there.

blocks.caption: Without a cache, every request makes the application server query the database again (repeated work). With a cache: on a cache miss, the data is fetched from the database and stored; on a cache hit, the stored result is reused.

blocks.text: Caching tools: Memcached and Redis. Both keep data in memory as key–value pairs.

blocks.caption: Redis and Memcached store results of common operations in memory, reducing repeated database work.

blocks.text: Levels of caching (chapter)

blocks.caption: The three levels of caching: (1) browser cache — the browser reuses stored website files (CSS, JS, images); (2) server cache — the application server reuses stored data or pages; (3) database query cache — the database reuses results of recent unchanged queries.

blocks.text: Caching can happen at three levels:
Web browser cache. The browser keeps copies of previously visited pages and checks whether the page has changed. If the page has not changed, it can use its cached copy.
Web server — page cache. The web server stores generated pages and can send a stored page to the client without going to the database.
Database — query cache. The database keeps the results of recent queries that have not changed, and returns them without re-running the query.
7.2 Task queues (asynchronous work queues)
As a website grows, some tasks become resource- and time-consuming:
sending emails or notifications to thousands of users;
bulk creating or updating database records. For example, deleting a user means deleting all data associated with that user.
These tasks need not be done immediately. The user can be told that the task will be carried out, and notified later when it is complete.
The problem with the normal request–response cycle

Normally: the user sends a request (“send an email to my friend”) → the server processes it and actually sends the email → the server responds “email sent”. The user waits the whole time. For one email that is fine. For thousands, it is not scalable, because nobody can wait that long for a response.
The solution: an asynchronous work queue
Section point: An asynchronous work queue executes tasks outside the normal HTTP request–response cycle. It consists of:
a queue of jobs to be performed, along with their parameters, and
a pool of workers that take jobs from the queue and perform them.
The server just adds a job to the queue and responds to the user immediately. The workers do the slow work in the background.

blocks.caption: Synchronous vs asynchronous: synchronously, the Flask server saves the order, sends the email, and only then confirms, so the customer waits; asynchronously, it saves the order, puts an email task in the task queue, responds immediately, and a background worker sends the email.

blocks.text: Why a pool of workers?
Many workers share the work, so the jobs are finished in much less time than with a single worker.
If you expect higher traffic than usual, you can dynamically increase the number of workers so jobs still finish quickly.

blocks.caption: Task queue and worker pool: the application records the order and creates background jobs; jobs (Email A, B, C) wait in the task queue; several workers take jobs in parallel and send the confirmation emails.

blocks.text: 7.3 Loading and rendering pages quickly
Web applications contain a lot of static content: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images. These must load quickly.
Why does a few seconds matter?
User stress: the chapter shows research that the stress caused by mobile page delays is comparable to watching a horror movie. Even a few extra seconds of loading make us uncomfortable and agitated.
Business impact (chapter examples, worth remembering):
2016 — AliExpress made its site 30% faster → customer orders rose 10.5%.
2006 — Google slowed its search results by half a second → user requests dropped 25%.
Method 1 — Minify the code

Minify = remove unnecessary whitespace and comments, and sometimes shorten names, while preserving program behaviour. Required separators and whitespace inside string values must be preserved. A minifier can also shorten names (such as parameter names). The code still does exactly the same thing; it is just smaller.
Section example: a small JavaScript function that converts Fahrenheit to Celsius.

(The code above illustrates the idea; the chapter’s exact snippet came from DigitalOcean’s minify tool.) For the chapter’s small function, minifying saved about 41% of the size. Across a whole website this adds up to a large saving, so pages load faster.

blocks.caption: Minification: readable HTML, CSS and JS with comments, whitespace and formatting go through a minifier, which removes unnecessary characters while keeping the intended behaviour, producing smaller files and less data to transfer.

blocks.text: Method 2 — Compress static pages

Tools such as Gzip and Brotli compress web pages and other resources before sending them. The browser decompresses them on arrival, and the original content is restored exactly, because the compression is lossless.

blocks.caption: Gzip and Brotli: the web server compresses HTML, CSS and JS losslessly, the compressed response travels over the network (fewer bytes), and the browser decompresses it so the original content is restored and the site displays normally.

blocks.text: Minification vs compression: the two are different and are used together. Minification rewrites the code itself to remove unneeded characters. Compression encodes the bytes for transfer and is undone by the browser.
Why monitor after deployment?

Section point: Even after thorough testing in the testing and staging environments, issues can still arise in the live environment. The application must therefore be constantly monitored once deployed.

blocks.caption: Application monitoring: the live application in production sends monitoring data (CPU, memory, requests, errors) to a dashboard; warning signs are detected; the team investigates and responds; monitoring continues over time.

blocks.text: What to monitor (chapter)
CPU utilisation: how it behaves, especially at peak times.
Memory utilisation.
Storage: consumed vs free. If database-heavy activity fills the disk, nothing new can be added to the database, and users start getting errors.
Network bandwidth and latency. Latency is the time it takes for a user to get a response. Check periodically that it is not getting worse.

blocks.caption: Monitoring CPU (processing load), memory (RAM consumption), storage (disk capacity used by application, log and database files) and network activity (incoming and outgoing data transfer) of the cloud VM running the shop.

A monitoring dashboard: (1) in normal operation the metrics are within the expected range; (2) warning signs appear — CPU rising, slow responses, more errors; (3) the team investigates by comparing trends, inspecting logs and checking the application.

blocks.text: Monitoring tools — 1: Reporting tools (Lighthouse)
Reporting tools generate reports. You give them a URL, and they:
analyse the page’s resources,
give optimisation suggestions,
check metrics such as SEO and accessibility, and
calculate a performance score for the website.

Section point: Lighthouse is a tool provided by Google. The chapter describes it as a Google Chrome extension that you can install to check the performance scores of websites. The chapter demonstrates it on the verisim.tech website, showing metrics such as how long the page takes to load and the Speed Index.

blocks.caption: Google Lighthouse: the Chrome extension demonstrated on verisim.tech reports performance scores, loading time and Speed Index, with suggestions for improvement.
blocks.alt: Google Lighthouse Chrome extension analysing verisim.tech, showing performance score, page loading time, Speed Index, SEO and accessibility.

blocks.text: Monitoring tools — 2: Understanding customer behaviour
Monitoring is not only about servers. Another important reason to monitor is to understand how customers behave. These ideas belong to web analytics.

blocks.caption: Web analytics: visitors browse, view and add products; the site records relevant events (page view, product click, add to cart) in a privacy-aware way; the analytics dashboard shows visitors, popular pages and shopping journeys; the team makes data-informed improvements and measures again.

blocks.text: The chapter names three things to monitor.
(a) Clickstreams

Section point: Clickstreams answer the question: which sequences of pages do your users visit the most? A website offers many possible paths, and clickstream analysis shows which paths users actually take most often.

blocks.caption: User clickstream: Home page (page view) → Browse products (product click) → View product (product page view) → Add to cart → Checkout (checkout page view). The recorded sequence of actions helps the team understand the user journey.

blocks.text: (b) Think time / Dwell time
Section point: Think time or dwell time is how long a typical user stays on a given page.

blocks.caption: Dwell time and engagement: when a visitor arrives on a page, the time they spend and their interactions (scroll, click, add to cart) are recorded and analysed for engagement patterns.

blocks.text: (c) Abandonment
An application has flows: sequences of steps that lead to a goal. The chapter’s example is a purchase flow:
Product page → Buy Now → Add address → Add payment details → Pay
Section point: Abandonment = the percentage of users who “abandon” a flow instead of completing it.
Completing the flow is the desired path for the business. Abandoning it partway means lost business from that customer, which is why abandonment is an important metric to monitor.

blocks.caption: Shopping cart abandonment: a user views the product, adds it to the cart, then leaves without buying. The shopping funnel (product view → add to cart → checkout → purchase) shows where users drop off; adding to cart does not mean a purchase.

blocks.text: Analytics tools — Google Analytics

Section point: Analytics tools work by embedding a small piece of JavaScript in every page of your website. This snippet contains a tracking code, and it sends information to the analytics tool each time the page is loaded. Google Analytics is the example. It shows metrics such as what happens after each interaction and where users drop off. To use it, you sign up for an account and insert the tracking code into your website.

blocks.caption: Analytics tools: a tracking code in every page
blocks.alt: Analytics tools: a tracking code in every page

blocks.text: Monitoring for A/B testing
Suppose version A of your website has a problem. For example, abandonment is high. To fix it you create version B, with a new workflow or a better UI.
How do you know whether B is actually better? The chapter’s answer is to:
Use a canary deployment (phased / incremental rollout), so that some users get version A and other users get version B.
Monitor both versions and check which one is better.
“Better” can be measured as more traffic, more dwell time on a page, more sales, less abandonment, and so on.

Section point: Monitoring is useful for A/B testing: checking whether the new version of your application is better than the previous one. In the chapter, the A/B split is done using a canary-style incremental rollout.

blocks.caption: Monitoring for A/B testing using a canary rollout
blocks.alt: Monitoring for A/B testing using a canary rollout

blocks.text: Summary of Parts 7 and 8

rows: Store results of common operations in memory; reduces server load; Memcached, Redis; levels: browser, web server (page cache), database (query cache)
For time-consuming tasks (bulk emails, bulk DB updates); asynchronous, outside the HTTP request–response cycle; queue of jobs + parameters, pool of workers; workers can be increased dynamically
Matters for users (stress) and business (AliExpress 30% faster → +10.5% orders; Google +0.5 s → −25% requests); minify code (~41% saved in example); compress with Gzip/Brotli
CPU, memory, storage (consumed vs free), network bandwidth, latency
Lighthouse (Google): page resources, suggestions, SEO, accessibility, performance score
Clickstreams (most common page sequences), think/dwell time (time on a page), abandonment (% who leave a flow)
JavaScript tracking code embedded in every page; e.g. Google Analytics
Version A vs B rolled out via canary; monitor which is better (traffic, dwell time, sales, abandonment)

blocks.text: Try each question before reading the answer.
Q1. Which environment is described as “an exact replica of production, running on a remote machine”? Answer: The staging (pre-production) environment.

Q2. Give the three reasons the chapter offers for using a staging environment. Answer: (1) Deployment involves many activities and configurations, and doing it directly in production could crash the live system and affect users. (2) To preview new features to management, sales/marketing or clients. (3) To do performance and stress testing without affecting real users.

Q3. In the testing environment, what happens when a test fails? Answer: The defective code is removed, the failing module and its developer are identified and the developer is notified, the code is rolled back to the previous working version, and the developer fixes the bug in their working copy and recommits it for the next scheduled deployment.

Q4. What is the main advantage of blue/green deployment? Answer: Easy rollback. If the new (green) environment has problems, the router sends users back to the old (blue) environment, which still works.

Q5. What are the other names for canary deployment, and what is its drawback? Answer: Phased rollout or incremental rollout. Drawback: you must manage multiple instances (old and new versions) at once.
Q6. Name three ways of selecting users for a canary rollout. Answer: Randomly; based on user profile or demographics; based on region.

Q7. A mobile app keeps old versions running and lets users decide whether to update. Which strategy is this, and what is its drawback? Answer: Versioned deployment. Drawback: the company has to maintain multiple versions.
Q8. An IaaS provider has a server with an 8-core CPU and 32 GB RAM and slices it into 8 VMs. What does each VM get? Answer: 1 core and 4 GB of memory.
Q9. Match each option with its advantage: Bare metal, IaaS, PaaS. Answer: Bare metal → highest performance; IaaS → cheaper, no maintenance; PaaS → very easy to deploy.
Q10. What is the main disadvantage of PaaS? Answer: Lack of control over the underlying OS, hardware and configuration.
Q11. Classify each provider as IaaS or PaaS: DigitalOcean, Heroku, AWS (EC2), Google App Engine, Linode. Answer: IaaS: DigitalOcean, AWS, Linode. PaaS: Heroku, Google App Engine.
Q12. What is a “Droplet”? Answer: DigitalOcean’s name for a virtual machine.

Q13. Which two files must be prepared before deploying a Flask app to Heroku, and what does each do? Answer: requirements.txt lists the required packages and versions, which Heroku installs. The Procfile tells Heroku how to run the app (e.g. web: gunicorn app:app).
Q14. What is Gunicorn? Answer: A WSGI (Web Server Gateway Interface) server that Heroku uses to run Python web applications.
Q15. In the Heroku tutorial, which command uploads the code and triggers deployment? Answer: git push heroku master. Heroku is set up as a git remote.

Q16. List the seven best practices of continuous integration. Answer: (1) Maintain a single source repository; (2) automate the build; (3) make the build self-testing; (4) commit to the main branch every day; (5) every commit should build the main branch on an integration server; (6) fix broken builds immediately; (7) automate deployment.

Q17. Why should developers commit every day? Answer: Infrequent commits increase the chance of conflict errors. Frequent commits encourage breaking work into small chunks, keep conflicts small, and avoid a last-minute rush before releases.
Q18. How is a broken build fixed immediately? Answer: Take the system back to the last-known good build, then fix the bug.
Q19. Name two CI servers and two build tools from the chapter. Answer: CI servers: Jenkins, CruiseControl. Build tools: Ant, Gradle (Java) and “Builder” (Node.js).
Q20. State one drawback of continuous integration. Answer: The initial effort to set up processes and the integration server, and to train people.
Q21. Name the three levels at which caching can happen. Answer: Web browser cache, web server page cache, database query cache.

Q22. Why is an asynchronous task queue used for sending emails to thousands of users? Answer: Doing it inside the normal request–response cycle would make the user wait far too long and does not scale. The job is put in a queue and a pool of workers processes it in the background, outside the HTTP request–response cycle. More workers can be added when traffic is high.
Q23. What two things does an asynchronous work queue consist of? Answer: A queue of jobs (with their parameters) and a pool of workers.

Q24. What does minification do, and how is it different from compression? Answer: Minification removes spaces, tabs, extra whitespace and comments (and can shorten names) from the code itself without changing behaviour. Compression (Gzip, Brotli) encodes the files into fewer bytes for transfer, and the browser decompresses them.
Q25. According to the chapter, what happened when Google slowed search results by half a second in 2006? Answer: User requests dropped by 25%.
Q26. List four things to monitor in a live application. Answer: CPU utilisation, memory utilisation, storage (consumed vs free), and network bandwidth and latency.
Q27. What is latency? Answer: The time it takes for a user to get a response.
Q28. What does Lighthouse report on? Answer: It analyses page resources, suggests optimisations, checks SEO and accessibility, and calculates a performance score.

Q29. Define clickstream, dwell time and abandonment. Answer: Clickstream: the sequences of pages users visit, and which are most common. Dwell (think) time: how long a typical user stays on a given page. Abandonment: the percentage of users who leave a flow (e.g. a purchase) instead of completing it.

Q30. How does an analytics tool such as Google Analytics collect data? Answer: A small JavaScript snippet containing a tracking code is embedded in every page. It sends information to the analytics tool each time a page loads.

Q31. How does the chapter suggest running an A/B test, and what counts as “better”? Answer: Use a canary (phased/incremental) rollout so some users get version A and others version B, then monitor both. “Better” can mean more traffic, more dwell time, more sales or less abandonment.
Abandonment: percentage of users who start a flow (e.g. checkout) but do not complete it.
A/B testing: showing version A to some users and version B to others, and comparing which performs better.
Bare metal server: physical server hardware that you buy and manage yourself.
Blue/Green deployment: two production environments; the router switches all users from the old (blue) to the new (green); easy rollback.
Build tool: software that automates compiling, copying files and creating schemas (Ant, Gradle).
Cache: a fast store of reusable results in memory.
Canary deployment: rolling out a new version gradually to a small subset of users first (phased/incremental rollout).
Clickstream: the sequence of pages a user visits.
Continuous Integration (CI): automating the integration and deployment of software.
CI server: a server that monitors the repository and automatically builds and tests each commit (Jenkins, CruiseControl).
Deployment: placing the software so that users can access it.
Deployment strategy: a planned way of moving code from staging to production.
Droplet: DigitalOcean’s name for a virtual machine.
Dwell time / think time: how long a user stays on a page.
Environment: a system (or set of systems) that executes a software application.
Gunicorn: a WSGI server used to run Python web apps (used by Heroku).
Gzip / Brotli: lossless compression for web resources.
Hosting: the infrastructure on which an application is deployed.
IaaS (Infrastructure-as-a-Service): renting virtual machines from a provider (DigitalOcean, AWS, Linode).
Latency: the time taken for a user to receive a response.
Lighthouse: Google’s tool for auditing page performance, SEO and accessibility.
Mainline / master branch: the shared code base in version control.
Minification: removing unnecessary characters from code to make it smaller.
Monitoring: capturing and analysing an application’s execution information.
PaaS (Platform-as-a-Service): a platform that runs your application for you (Heroku, Google App Engine).
Procfile: a Heroku file stating how to start the app.
Production environment: the live environment used by real users.
requirements.txt: a list of Python packages and versions needed by a project.
Rollback: returning to the previous working version.
SSH: Secure Shell, an encrypted way to log in to a remote machine.
Staging environment: pre-production environment that exactly resembles production; runs on a remote machine.
Task queue (asynchronous work queue): a queue of jobs processed by a pool of workers outside the request–response cycle.
Testing environment: where integration and system testing are done.
Tracking code: a JavaScript snippet that sends page-visit data to an analytics tool.
Versioned deployment: keeping all versions alive and letting users choose which to use.
Virtual machine (VM): a software-defined computer carved out of a physical server.
Working copy: a developer’s local copy of the code base.
